title: Kindness and the retest
hookLine: self-compassion after a failure increased motivation to improve (Breines and Chen)
carry: self-compassion after a slip fuels trying again

lines: KIND WORDS, A PEP TALK, OR NOTHING.
cards: A test comes back, and it went badly. It was a hard one, and the score shows it. The next few minutes happen mostly inside the student's head: a shrug, a pep talk, or a quiet list of everything wrong with them.
The psychologists Juliana Breines and Serena Chen set up that exact moment. Some students were offered a few kind words, some a boost to their self-esteem, some nothing at all.
Then each could study for a retest, and the researchers watched how long they kept at it. The same moment comes after any slip.

teach.h: HARSHNESS MAKES IT HARD TO LOOK.
teach.b: In the test study, the kind words were simple: tests like this are hard for lots of students, so try not to be too hard on yourself.

Given the chance to study for a retest, the students who read them studied longer than the self-esteem group or the group that got nothing. In another study, people recalled something they had done wrong.

Those prompted toward self-compassion were more motivated to make amends and not repeat it. Second, why it might work. Harsh self-talk can make a lapse feel like a threat, and threats are easier to look away from.
Kindness makes it safer to look at what went wrong.

The psychologist Kristin Neff describes self-compassion in three parts: kindness instead of harsh judgment, remembering that failing is part of being human, and noticing the pain without drowning in it.
Self-compassion isn't letting yourself off the hook. In Breines and Chen's work, it went with more effort to improve, not less. Fourth, an old line.
The book of Leviticus says, "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." It is first a command about the neighbor. Some readers also hear in it a quiet assumption that the self is cared for too.
Gentleness turned inward isn't softness. It's what lets someone get up and try again.

how: People who practice self-compassion often answer a slip the way they would answer a friend's, naming that it hurt and that slips are common, and then take one small step back toward their plan.

games.q: what does “kind after a lapse” mean?
o: letting yourself off the hook so the slip doesn't matter
pumping up your self-esteem after something goes wrong
meeting a slip with understanding, which helps you try again

games.q: inside kind after a lapse: tap the pairs.

s: self-compassion means letting yourself off the hook
in Breines and Chen's work, it went with more effort to improve.
after recalling a wrong, self-compassion went with wanting to make amends
those prompted toward self-compassion were more motivated to make amends.
a self-esteem boost worked just as well before the retest

games.q: you've just done badly on a hard test. which response led to more studying in Breines and Chen's work?
o: 'tests like this are hard; go easy on yourself.'
games.why: the self-compassion words went with longer studying than a self-esteem boost or nothing at all.

practice: Bring to mind one small slip from this week, not the biggest one, and notice what the inner voice says about it.
Then try the three parts quietly: this stung; people slip like this; and, in plain words, what you'd say to a friend who slipped the same way. Then let it go and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Kind after a lapse. Meeting a slip with understanding instead of harshness, which in research went with more effort to improve, not less. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: self-compassion after a slip fuels trying again. A slip met gently is easier to learn from. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Neff, "Self-compassion: An alternative conceptualization of a healthy attitude toward oneself"
